current_episode.title: #57 - Unlocking College Athletic Scholarships: Insider Recruiting Strategies with Renee Lopez

guest.titre: Author, College Coach, Speaker and Trainer
guest.bio_context: Renee Lopez served as a college coach for 14 years, holding positions as a D1 head coach, D2 head coach, and NAI head coach. She also worked as an NCAA compliance director, giving her unique insight into both coaching and rule enforcement. She founded a Facebook group that grew to over 260,000 parents supporting families through the college athletic recruiting process, and authored the book 'Looking for a Full Ride' based on interviews with 65 college coaches and athletic directors across 19 sports.

And so I was actually going through the process where I would do presentations all the time with families and talking to different schools and clubs and school counselors and coaches about the college recruiting process, what to do, what not to do. So we actually started the process of putting the book together and in the midst of it continued doing consulting and lots of speaking engagements across the country. pending_qa.q: Is attending a specialized high school or academy like IMG Academy necessary to get recruited for college athletics?
pending_qa.r: Absolutely not. College coaches want talented players who are challenged, whether through club teams, travel teams, or even a less talented high school program where you can demonstrate leadership. You can market yourself through highlight films, emailing coaches with videos, and inviting them to your games. Families do not need to move or pay thousands of dollars for a specialized school to be evaluated.

pending_qa.q: What are the key misconceptions athletes and families have about the college recruiting process?
pending_qa.r: A common misconception is that you must know somebody or that someone has to know somebody to be recruited. In reality, student-athletes can reach out directly to college coaches to express interest and get evaluated through video and live play. Additionally, many people overemphasize rankings like blue-chip or five-star status, when college coaches are primarily evaluating film, live performance, and whether you fit academically, athletically, socially, and financially with their program.

pending_qa.q: How should families approach the decision of whether their child should specialize in one sport or play multiple sports during high school?
pending_qa.r: Multiple college coaches prioritize rest and recovery as the number one concern. While some athletes can play multiple sports, the key is managing schedules to ensure mental and physical breaks, protect mental health, maintain academics, and prevent overuse injuries like ACLs. The approach should depend on family schedules and what can be realistically managed without sacrificing overall wellbeing.

pending_qa.q: What inspired Renee Lopez to transition from college coaching to building resources for the college recruiting process?
pending_qa.r: After coaching for 14 years—a lifestyle career requiring about 80 hours per week—Lopez felt God moving her in a different direction. She began doing recruiting seminars for high schools, counselors, and clubs, with people repeatedly urging her to write a book. She interviewed 65 college coaches and athletic directors across 19 sports to bridge the gap between what college coaches actually want and what student-athletes think they want, while also ensuring families had accurate, up-to-date NCAA information.

pending_qa.q: How has the Facebook group for college recruiting guidance grown and what value does it provide to families?
pending_qa.r: The Facebook group, 'Educating Parents of High School Athletes on the College Recruiting Process,' grew from initial COVID-era webinars and now has over 260,000 members. Growth came through word of mouth as members invited others. The group provides free information to help families understand they do not need to hire expensive recruiting services. It teaches families to learn and implement the process themselves, helping hundreds of students commit to college programs and find the right fit while prioritizing education, career goals, social fit, and mental health.

pending_qa.q: How does John Maxwell leadership training complement Renee Lopez's work in college recruiting and business consulting?
pending_qa.r: After reading John Maxwell's books and implementing leadership principles with college teams, Lopez became certified as a John Maxwell trainer. This allows her to work across industries—sports teams, churches, Fortune 500 companies, schools, and medical fields—teaching team dynamics, personality assessment using DISC training, and leadership development. She applies the principle that team dynamics are universal regardless of industry, helping leaders grow their own leadership to support those following them.
